newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: FEATURE - Last Cambodian forest refuge under threat.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Last Cambodian forest refuge under threat.

text.p: In a secluded clearing deep inside this Cambodian national park, jagged piles of fresh-cut wood are scattered on the forest floor and smoke drifts from smouldering elephant grass.
Minister of Environment Mok Mareth, a tall, soft-spoken man, surveys the scene of destruction like a grim general.
"There were ten sawmills here," he says, "but now they are finished."

Earlier in February, Mok Mareth explains, ministry staff flying over the park, located 100 kilometres (60 miles) southwest of Phnom Penh, noticed the covert saw mills and ordered soldiers in to shut down the operation.
It was a success, but unfortunately only a minor victory in a major war, environmental officials say.
ILLEGAL LOGGING THREATENS DWINDLING FORESTS
They warn that illegal logging is thriving in Cambodia's last protected areas, threatening dwindling wildlife and forests.
And other government officials said on Monday that logging continues unabated in Cambodia despite a government directive banning all log exports from December 31.
"The parks are already jeopardised," says one high-placed environmental official, who describes the scale of the problem as "unbelievable."
He said bandits but also military that guard the parks are often involved in the illegal logging, making the recent success in carrying out an army-supported crackdown a rare one.
Defence officials acknowledge the problem, but say that with salaries of only $20 to $35 per month, army officers often sell the trees they are meant to protect.
Worse, the government has already conceded much of the forests outside of park areas to foreign companies, and loggers have sometimes infringed on protected areas, says Mok Mareth.

A World Bank and United Nations study of the problem determined that foreign demand, coupled with Cambodians' need for fuel wood and extra income, led to a loss of close to 1.4 million hectares (3.5 million acres) of forest between 1973 and 1993.
Those problems are clearly visible at Kirirom, home to one of Southeast Asia's last stands of native pine.
SAD DESTINY FOR HISTORICAL PARK
Dozens of roadside stalls leading into the park are selling logs and charcoal, and heavily armed soldiers are roving throughout the mountainous terrain.
Sawn-off stumps attest to the activity of the saw mills, which processed soft and hardwoods mostly for local construction use.
Mok Mareth says that is a sad destiny for a park where King Norodom Sihanouk explored the cool slopes by elephant in 1945 and tourists and foreign dignitaries vacationed in the 1960s.

The park then survived a 17-year occupation by Khmer Rouge guerrillas and was declared a protected area by Sihanouk in 1995, but may not outlast nearby logging concessions, illegal logging in the park and the decision to cede 1,500 hectares (3,700 acres) of the 10,000-hectare (24,700-acre) pine stand to a tea company.
Mok Mareth hopes additional aid from the United States, which funds an environmental consortium at the Ministry of Environment, might help.
But as donors, who supply about 40 percent of the national budget, become increasingly concerned about heavy logging, some are reluctant to fund a government viewed as part of the problem.
ENVIRONMENTALISTS HOPE PRESSURE WILL SAVE PARKS
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) last November cancelled a $20 million loan over concerns with the government's forestry policies and incomplete accounting for logging revenues.
An IMF team arrived on February 24 to revisit the issue and determine the fate of $40 million more in loans, a decision likely to influence future assistance from other agencies.

British environmental group Global Witness, in a briefing paper titled "A Tug of War, the struggle to preserve Cambodia's forests", has also criticised the government's management of "quasi-legal" logging concessions.
"Unfortunately, yes," said Minister of Finance Keat Chhon on Monday when asked whether charges from the environmental group were true.
"We have to work hard so that this government can organise its natural resources in a proper way," Keat Chhon told reporters after opening a seminar on trade.

Environmentalists hope the pressure will convince the government to save the country's seven national parks, 11 wildlife sanctuaries and five other protected areas -- if not the rest of the forests in this heavily wooded country.
"These areas are now protected on paper only," says Alan Robinson of the Cambodia Environmental Management Project, the consortium based at the Ministry of Environment.
"We need to undertake some immediate management and some long-term planning as soon as possible."
